# **Syllabus A1**

The German A1 syllabus—aligned with the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR)—is designed for absolute beginners to build foundational communication skills. It is divided into four core competencies supported by basic grammar and a vocabulary of roughly 500 to 800 words.  
**Core Topics & Vocabulary**

* **Personal Information:** Greetings, introductions, name, age, nationality, profession, and family members.  
* **Daily Life & Routine:** Telling time, days of the week, months, seasons, and daily activities.  
* **Shopping & Food:** Buying groceries, talking about prices, food items, and ordering at a restaurant or café.  
* **Travel & Environment:** Asking for directions, navigating public transport, and describing your home or neighborhood.  
* **Leisure:** Hobbies, sports, and expressing simple likes and dislikes.

**Fundamental Grammar**

* **Sentence Structure:** Basic word order in declarative statements, yes/no questions, and W-questions (*Wer? Was? Wo? Wie?*).  
* **Verbs:** Present tense conjugation of regular and irregular verbs, modal verbs (*können, wollen, müssen, möchten*), and separable/inseparable verbs.  
* **Articles & Nouns:** Definite (*der, die, das*) and indefinite (*ein, eine*) articles, plural forms, and basic negation using *nicht* and *kein*.  
* **Cases:** Nominative and basic Accusative/Dative cases, along with common prepositions of place and time.  
* **Pronouns:** Personal pronouns (*ich, du, er/sie/es*) and basic possessive pronouns (*mein, dein*).

**Exam Structure (e.g., Goethe-Zertifikat A1 / TELC A1)**

* **Listening (\~20 mins):** Understanding short, slow audio clips like public announcements, answer phone messages, or simple dialogues.  
* **Reading (\~25 mins):** Comprehending brief notes, classified ads, signs, posters, and simple emails.  
* **Writing (\~20 mins):** Filling out basic forms with personal details and writing a short, simple message or email.  
* **Speaking (\~15 mins):** Introducing yourself, formulating basic questions, and responding to everyday prompts.

# **Syllabus A1 (3)**

Acquiring Mastery in  the German A1 level is the first step towards fluency in the German language. This level is designed for beginners who have little to no prior knowledge of the language. Here, we provide a detailed breakdown of the German A1 syllabus, ensuring learners understand what to expect and how to prepare effectively.

### Understanding the German A1 Syllabus

### What is the German A1 Syllabus?

The German A1 syllabus is the foundation for learning German at a beginner level. It follows the CEFR (Common European Framework of Reference for Languages) and helps learners develop basic communication skills. This guide covers all essential A1 German topics, vocabulary, and grammar.

The German A1 syllabus is structured to build foundational language skills. This includes basic grammar, vocabulary, speaking, reading, listening, and writing. The primary focus is to enable learners to communicate in everyday situations with simple sentences. The German A1 syllabus is designed for beginners and focuses on developing basic language skills. It includes learning essential vocabulary and grammar structures, such as greetings, numbers, and simple sentence construction. Key topics include introducing oneself, talking about daily routines, shopping, and ordering food. 

The German A1 level emphasizes comprehension of simple texts, basic conversations, and understanding common phrases in everyday situations. Grammar topics cover present tense verbs, articles, and personal pronouns. By the end of the course, learners will be able to understand and use familiar expressions in basic German conversations. The German A1 syllabus provides a solid foundation for further language learning.  

![German A1 Syllabus][image1]

###  

### Key Components of the German A1 Level

1\. German A1 Vocabulary:

In the A1 level German syllabus, learners are expected to acquire a vocabulary of approximately 500–800 words. These words cover essential topics such as:

* Introductions and Personal Information: Name, age, nationality, profession.  
* Family and Relationships: Basic family terms like Mutter (mother), Vater (father), Bruder (brother), etc.  
* Everyday Activities: Shopping, dining, traveling, and hobbies.  
* Numbers and Time: Telling the time, days of the week, months, seasons.  
* Common Adjectives and Adverbs: Colors, sizes, and descriptions.

Expanding your vocabulary is crucial for effective communication. Here are key areas covered:

* Greetings & Introductions – Hallo, Guten Morgen, Wie geht’s?  
* Numbers & Dates – Eins, Zwei, Drei, Montag, Januar  
* Family & Relationships – Mutter, Vater, Geschwister, Freund  
* Food & Drinks – Brot, Wasser, Kaffee, Obst  
* Daily Routine – Aufstehen, Schlafen, Arbeiten, Lernen  
* Shopping & Directions – Supermarkt, Bahnhof, rechts, links  
* Weather & Seasons – Sonne, Regen, Frühling, Winter

2\. German A1 Grammar:

The grammar section of the German A1 syllabus focuses on simple structures to build confidence in communication. Key grammar topics include:

* Nouns and Articles: Differentiating between definite (der, die, das) and indefinite (ein, eine) articles.  
* Pronouns: Personal pronouns like ich (I), du (you), er/sie/es (he/she/it), and possessive pronouns.  
* Verb Conjugation: Regular and irregular verbs in the present tense, including sein (to be) and haben (to have).  
* Sentence Structure: Subject-verb-object order and basic questions.  
* Prepositions: Usage of prepositions such as in, auf, unter.  
* Negation: Using nicht and kein to negate sentences.

Grammar forms the backbone of language learning. The A1 syllabus includes:

* Basic Sentence Structure – Subject-Verb-Object (Ich lerne Deutsch)  
* Present Tense (Präsens) – Ich bin, Du hast, Er lernt  
* Articles & Genders – Der, Die, Das (Definite & Indefinite Articles)  
* Personal Pronouns – Ich, Du, Er, Sie, Wir, Ihr  
* Negation (Nicht & Kein) – Ich habe kein Buch, Er arbeitet nicht  
* Basic Modal Verbs – Können, Müssen, Wollen  
* Prepositions – In, Auf, Unter, Neben

3\. Speaking & Listening Skills:

Listening and speaking skills are vital aspects of the German A1 level syllabus. Activities include:

* Understanding simple conversations about familiar topics.  
* Practicing greetings, introductions, and polite expressions.  
* Participating in role-play exercises for daily scenarios like ordering food or asking for directions.

Developing listening and speaking skills is essential for real-world conversations. The A1 syllabus covers:

* Simple Conversations – Introducing yourself, ordering in a restaurant  
* Asking Questions – Wie heißt du? Wo wohnst du?  
* Understanding Announcements – Train stations, supermarkets  
* Common Expressions & Idioms – Guten Tag, Viel Glück, Bis bald

4\. Reading & Writing in German:

Reading exercises are designed to help learners understand short and simple texts. These include:

* Reading advertisements, notices, or emails.  
* Identifying main ideas and keywords in a text.  
* Following simple instructions.

Writing at the A1 level focuses on creating basic sentences and short paragraphs. Examples include:

* Writing about oneself, such as hobbies, family, or daily routine.  
* Filling out forms with personal information.  
* Composing brief messages or emails.

A1 learners will build skills in reading comprehension and basic writing:

* Reading Short Texts – Emails, signs, menus, invitations  
* Writing Simple Sentences – Mein Name ist Anna. Ich wohne in Berlin.  
* Filling Forms – Name, Adresse, Geburtsdatum

### Detailed Breakdown of Learning Units for A1-level German program 

Unit 1: Personal Introductions This unit introduces learners to:

* Basic phrases for self-introduction.  
* Asking and answering questions about name, age, and nationality.  
* Common verbs like heißen (to be called) and wohnen (to live).

Unit 2: Daily Routines In German A1 syllabus, learners explore vocabulary and grammar related to:

* Everyday activities like eating, working, and leisure.  
* Using the present tense to describe routines.  
* Expressing likes and dislikes using mögen (to like).

Unit 3: Shopping and Dining This unit equips learners with:

* Vocabulary for groceries, clothing, and restaurants.  
* Polite requests and questions (e.g., "Haben Sie…?" or "Wie viel kostet…?").  
* Currency and numbers.

Unit 4: Travel and Directions Topics covered include:

* Common travel phrases and transportation vocabulary.  
* Asking for and understanding directions.  
* Reading maps and signs.

Unit 5: Family and Friends In German language A1 syllabus,this include:

* Describing family members and relationships.  
* Talking about celebrations and events.  
* Using possessive pronouns effectively.

### Best Study Tips for German A1 Learners

1\. Use German Language Apps:

Apps like Duolingo, Babbel, and Anki help reinforce vocabulary and grammar.

2\. Watch German Videos:

Beginner-friendly videos on YouTube enhance listening skills.

3\. Practice Speaking Daily:

Speak with native speakers or join language exchange programs.

4\. Read Simple Texts:

Children’s books and basic German newspapers help improve reading skills.

5\. Take a German A1 Course:

Enroll in online courses or attend Goethe-Institut classes for structured learning.

### Other important Tips to become proficient

Practice Daily: 

Consistency is key. Dedicate at least 30 minutes daily to practicing vocabulary and grammar.

1. Use Flashcards: Build your vocabulary with flashcards for quick revision.  
2. Listen to German Audio: Engage with beginner-level podcasts or videos to improve listening skills.  
3. Speak Regularly: Join language exchange groups or practice speaking with a tutor.  
4. Take Mock Tests: Familiarize yourself with the structure of A1-level exams like the Goethe-Zertifikat.

### Exam Preparation for Entry-level German syllabus:

The German A1 syllabus is the foundation for exams like Goethe-Zertifikat A1 and TELC A1. These exams typically consist of four sections:

* Listening: Answer questions based on short audio clips.  
* Reading: Comprehend and analyze simple texts.  
* Writing: Write brief paragraphs or fill out forms.  
* Speaking: Engage in a short conversation or present oneself.

## Important Q & A

### 1\. What are the topics for letter writing in A1 level German language?  

Here are some examples of German A1-syllabus email writing topics rephrased:

1. Responding to an Invitation:   
   Write an email to accept or decline an invitation, providing reasons for your decision.  
2. Planning a Visit:   
   Compose an email expressing your desire to visit a friend or inviting your friend to visit you.  
3. Scheduling an Appointment:   
   Write an email to book an appointment for a specific date and time.  
4. Excuse for Absence:   
   Draft an email to your teacher explaining why you will not be able to attend class.  
5. Request for Assistance:   
   Write an email asking someone for help, such as with shopping or another activity.  
6. Party Invitation:   
   Compose an email inviting your friend to attend your party.  
7. Inquiring About a City Visit:   
   Write an email requesting information about a city you plan to visit.  
8. Request for Information:   
   Draft an email to inquire about hotel bookings, details about a specific area, or renting a room or apartment.

# **Syllabus a1 (4)**

## **German A1 Syllabus** 

The German language A1 level syllabus is broken down into four essential skills. Four skills that are involved include listening, speaking, reading, and writing along with foundational grammar

**What you will learn at A1 level German:**

* **German A1 Grammar**  
* **German A1 Vocabulary**  
* **German A1 Speaking**  
* **German A1 Listening**  
* **German A1 Reading**  
* **German A1 Writing**

 

### **Listening**

* Accurate understanding of everyday spoken language in familiar situations like greetings, introductions, and shopping.   
* Ability to comprehend simple, deliberate speech in common contexts.   
* Listening to short phrases and practicing with exercises is often found in dialogues and announcements at train stations and shops.   
* Proficiency in recognizing sounds, stress, and intonation patterns.   
* Recognition of specific words, phrases, and key information, such as names, numbers, prices, and time. 

 

### **Speaking**

* Introduce yourself and other people.   
* Share basic personal details such as name, age, and academic background.   
* Discuss everyday topics in a simple way. (Example: ordering food and asking for directions)  
* Express likes, dislikes, and preferences.   
* Use polite conversational expressions such as “please,” “thank you,” or “pardon” in the German language.

 

### **Reading**

* Comprehending simple texts, such as letters from friends, posters advertising local events, or services.  
* Read and interpret short and uncomplicated-length pictures such as schedules, menus, and timetables.   
* Identifying the specific details in written material (e.g., days, hours, location). 

 

### **Writing**

* Take notes or write a short message or an email regarding an event or something important (e.g., a proposal or an agreement on meeting schedules).   
* Fill out forms requesting personal information such as name, address, date of birth, and country of origin.   
* Write a few coherent sentences about what you like about yourself.

 

### **Grammar**

* **In nouns and articles:** singular and plural forms and grammatical genders (der, die, das, ein, eine): definite articles/b**estimmte Artikel** or indefinite articles/unbestimmte Artikel.  
* **Pronouns:** Personal pronouns (ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie) and possessive pronouns (mein, dein, sein, etc.)  
* **Verbs:** Conjugation of regular and irregular verbs in present tense. Modal verbs (können, wollen, and müssen); separable and inseparable verbs.  
* **Negation:** When employing ‘nicht’ and ‘kein’ to form negative sentences.  
* **Construction of Sentences:** The general sequence of the subject and verb in statements and yes/no questions; basic conjunctions such as ‘and’ or ‘but,’ among others.   
* **Prepositions**: common accusative and dative prepositions (in, on, under, next to, with)   
* **Adjectives:** basic adjective endings and basic comparison (e.g., good, beautiful, little).  
* **Numbers:** Cardinal numbers from 1 to 100 and ordinal numbers such as first, second, etc. 

 

### **Vocabulary**

* **Daily Life:** Greeting and introducing friends and family.  
* **Shopping and Food:** Basic vocabulary for shopping, goods, and prices  
* **Time and Dates:** Days of the week, months of the year, telling time & planning a schedule (official and unofficial), and fixing appointments.  
* **Transportation and Directions:** Public transport, asking for directions, and navigating when lost.  
* **Hobbies and Leisure:** Talking about likes and dislikes and how often you do certain activities.

 

### **Culture**

* Basic facts about the German-speaking countries such as Germany, Austria, and Switzerland.   
* An introduction to German culture, traditions, and festivals (for example, Oktoberfest or Christmas markets). 

 

### **A1 Exam Format: an overview**

Usually, A1-type examinations such as the **Goethe-Zertifikat A**1 or TELC A1 include the following components: 

* **Listening:** Understanding short-format texts.  
* **Speaking:** Self-introduction, picture description, and simple answers to questions.  
* **Reading:** Reading a short text or forms and answering simple questions about it.  
* **Writing: C**omposing short pieces such as emails, postcards, or notes.

At the end of the A1 level, learners can understand and use familiar and simple used phrases and expressions in simple interactions. 

If you are seeking to obtain a **German A1 certificate**, [**the A1 German exam**](https://kochiva.com/blog/how-to-clear-german-a1-exam/) tests the four language fundamentals: listening, speaking, reading, and writing.
